# 01 · What is a skill?

> **Time:** 5 minutes · **You need:** nothing installed · **Prev:** [Home](../README.md) · **Next:** [02 · Install OpenCode](02-install-opencode.md)

## The one-sentence definition

A **skill** is a folder containing a `SKILL.md` file that teaches an agent a repeatable workflow, and that the agent loads only when the task needs it.

That is the whole concept. There is no registry, no build step, no daemon.

```text
.opencode/skills/hello-skill/
└── SKILL.md
```

```markdown
---
name: Hello Skill
description: Use when the user asks for a friendly greeting or a demo of skills
---

# Hello Skill

1. Greet the user by name.
2. Say which file you loaded.
```

## Why skills exist

Agents are good at reasoning and bad at remembering *your* way of doing things. Without a skill you repeat yourself every session:

> "No, the changelog goes above the diff, use `### Added` headers, and don't bump the patch version for docs-only changes."

A skill turns that into a file the agent reads on its own. One sentence in a `description`, and the knowledge is available forever — to you and to everyone who clones the repo.

## The two-part trick: advertise, then load

This is the part beginners miss, and it explains most "why isn't my skill doing anything" confusion.

```text
Every model step                          When the task matches
┌─────────────────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────────────┐
│ Available skills:           │          │ Full SKILL.md body           │
│  • hello-skill — Use when…  │  ──────► │ + base directory             │
│  • git-release — Prepare…   │  loads   │ + up to 10 supporting paths  │
│  • pdf-handling — Use when… │          │                              │
└─────────────────────────────┘          └──────────────────────────────┘
        names + descriptions only              instructions, on demand
```

1. **Advertise.** At every step, OpenCode gives the model a list of skills — **ID, name, description only**. Not the body.
2. **Load.** When your request matches a description (or you write `@skill-id`), the model calls the `skill` tool, and only then does the body enter the conversation.

Consequences worth internalizing:

- Many skills are cheap. Bodies are not in context until used.
- **A skill with no `description` is never advertised.** It still exists and can be loaded by ID, but the agent will not discover it.
- **Descriptions compete.** Two skills both claiming "use for code review" make the choice ambiguous. Write descriptions that describe a *situation*.
- Supporting files (`references/`, `scripts/`) are **not** loaded automatically. The body must tell the agent to read them.

## Anatomy of a real skill

```text
commit-message-writer/
├── SKILL.md                        ← required: frontmatter + instructions
├── references/
│   └── conventional-commits.md     ← read only when the skill says so
└── scripts/
    └── check-subject.sh            ← optional helper the agent can run
```

`SKILL.md` has two layers:

```markdown
---
name: Commit Message Writer                  ← display label (optional)
description: Use when writing a commit…      ← the trigger (this matters)
metadata:
  opencode/autoinvoke: true                  ← optional behavior switches
---

# Commit Message Writer                      ← body: plain Markdown

## When to use
## Workflow
## Rules
## Examples
```

| Frontmatter field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | Human-readable label. Defaults to the path-derived ID. |
| `description` | **The trigger.** Without it the model never sees the skill. |
| `metadata.opencode/autoinvoke: false` | Hide from the model's list; keep it loadable by ID. |
| `disable-model-invocation: true` | Same effect as above (portability alias). |

Everything else — `license`, `compatibility`, custom keys — is accepted but not interpreted by OpenCode.

## What a skill is *not*

| You might think… | Reality |
| --- | --- |
| "It's a plugin" | Plugins run code inside OpenCode. Skills are instructions the model reads. |
| "It's an MCP server" | MCP servers expose tools/data over a protocol. Skills teach procedure. |
| "It's an agent" | Agents are roles with their own model, tools, and permissions. Skills are procedures any agent can load. |
| "It's a slash command" | Commands are prompts *you* invoke. Skills are workflows the *model* invokes. |
| "It's a prompt file" | Close — but a skill has discovery, scoping, permissions, and supporting files. |

Longer comparison: [08 · Skills vs. agents vs. commands](08-skills-vs-agents-vs-commands.md).

## Where they live (preview)

| Scope | Path |
| --- | --- |
| Global | `~/.config/opencode/skills/<id>/SKILL.md` |
| Project | `.opencode/skills/<id>/SKILL.md` |
| Compatible | `~/.claude/skills/`, `~/.agents/skills/`, and project equivalents |
| Catalog | A URL in the `skills` array of `opencode.json` |

The ID is derived from the **path**, not the `name` field:

```text
.opencode/skills/git-release/SKILL.md   → id: git-release
.opencode/skills/teams/release/SKILL.md → id: release
```

---

## Check yourself

1. What are the only two things OpenCode shows the model before a skill is loaded?
2. Why does a skill with no `description` never trigger?
3. Your skill is at `.opencode/skills/My Skill/SKILL.md`. What ID do you type after `@`?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The skill's ID (and name) and its description.
2. Skills without a description are not advertised in the model's available list.
3. `My Skill` — IDs are path-derived and case-sensitive, spaces included. Which is exactly why the docs recommend lowercase kebab-case.
</details>

# 03 · Install a skill

> **Time:** 10 minutes · **Prev:** [02 · Install OpenCode](02-install-opencode.md) · **Next:** [04 · Use a skill](04-use-a-skill.md)

Installing a skill means **putting a folder where OpenCode looks**. That is the entire mechanism. Pick the route that fits you.

Before you start, decide the scope:

- **Global** → `~/.config/opencode/skills/` — your personal habits, available in every project.
- **Project** → `.opencode/skills/` — repo-specific commands and conventions, shared through git.

Not sure? [06 · Global vs. project](06-global-vs-project.md) has a decision table.

---

## Option 1 · CLI installer (easiest)

The [opencodeskills.dev](https://opencodeskills.dev/) installer reads the live catalog, lets you pick, and unpacks into the right folder. Node.js **20.12+** required.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://opencodeskills.dev/install.sh | sh
```

```powershell
# Windows PowerShell
irm https://opencodeskills.dev/cli.mjs -OutFile "$env:TEMP\opencode-skills.mjs"
node "$env:TEMP\opencode-skills.mjs"
```

Skip the menus by naming what you want:

```bash
# two skills, global
curl -fsSL https://opencodeskills.dev/install.sh | sh -s -- install xlsx pdf-handling

# into .opencode/skills/ of the current repo
curl -fsSL https://opencodeskills.dev/install.sh | sh -s -- install --project git-commits

# a whole category
curl -fsSL https://opencodeskills.dev/install.sh | sh -s -- install --category recommended --all

# search without installing
curl -fsSL https://opencodeskills.dev/install.sh | sh -s -- list excel
```

Useful flags: `--dir <path>` for a custom folder, `--yes` to skip confirmation in scripts.

---

## Option 2 · Download a zip

Every skill page on the directory has a `.zip`. For example:

```bash
curl -LO https://opencodeskills.dev/downloads/documentation/xlsx.zip
unzip -l xlsx.zip        # look before you extract
unzip xlsx.zip -d ~/.config/opencode/skills/
```

```powershell
# Windows: Expand-Archive, then move the inner folder
Invoke-WebRequest https://opencodeskills.dev/downloads/documentation/xlsx.zip -OutFile "$env:TEMP\xlsx.zip"
Expand-Archive "$env:TEMP\xlsx.zip" -DestinationPath "$env:TEMP\xlsx" -Force
Move-Item "$env:TEMP\xlsx\xlsx" "$HOME\.config\opencode\skills\xlsx" -Force
```

Result must be **exactly** one level deep:

```text
✅ ~/.config/opencode/skills/xlsx/SKILL.md
❌ ~/.config/opencode/skills/xlsx/xlsx/SKILL.md
```

> [!WARNING]
> The nested `xlsx/xlsx` path is the single most common install failure. It happens when you extract an archive that already contains a folder named after the skill **into** a folder with that same name.

---

## Option 3 · Load a catalog by URL (OpenCode 2)

Nothing is written to disk. Add a catalog to the `skills` array in `opencode.json`:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "skills": [
    "https://opencodeskills.dev/catalog/",
    "https://opencodeskills.dev/catalog/documentation/"
  ]
}
```

Put the file at `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` for every project, or at the repo root for one project. Restart the session; the skills appear alongside your local ones and download only when loaded.

Full explanation, including `index.json` mechanics: [07 · Load from a URL](07-load-from-url.md).

---

## Option 4 · By hand (no downloads, no Node)

This is also how you install **your own** skills.

```bash
# macOS / Linux — project scope
mkdir -p .opencode/skills/hello-skill
$EDITOR .opencode/skills/hello-skill/SKILL.md
```

```powershell
# Windows — project scope
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force .opencode\skills\hello-skill
notepad .opencode\skills\hello-skill\SKILL.md
```

Paste:

```markdown
---
name: Hello Skill
description: Use when the user asks for a friendly greeting or a demo of how skills work
---

# Hello Skill

1. Greet the user by name.
2. State the absolute path of the SKILL.md you loaded.
3. Ask one short follow-up question.
```

Step 2 is deliberate: it proves the agent read *your* file and not a hallucinated one.

---

## Confirm the install

1. **Start a new session.** Skills are discovered at session start.
2. Ask in a way that is easy to falsify:

```text
Load hello-skill and tell me its exact file path. Do not create any files.
```

3. Check the path matches what you installed.

If nothing happens, go to [09 · Troubleshooting](09-troubleshooting.md). The usual causes are a wrong filename, a nested folder, or a stale session.

## Update and remove

- **Update:** reinstall over the same folder. The CLI and unzip both overwrite.
- **Remove:** delete the skill's own folder.
- **Don't** delete the parent `skills/` folder — it removes every sibling skill too.

---

## Check yourself

1. Which scope does `.opencode/skills/` belong to, and who sees it?
2. You extracted a zip and got `xlsx/xlsx/SKILL.md`. What do you move?
3. Why does a catalog URL need no cleanup step?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Project scope — anyone who clones the repository.
2. Move the inner `xlsx` folder up one level so `SKILL.md` sits at `skills/xlsx/SKILL.md`.
3. Files are fetched on demand and never written to your skills folder.
</details>

# 04 · Use a skill

> **Time:** 10 minutes · **Prev:** [03 · Install a skill](03-install-a-skill.md) · **Next:** [05 · Write your first skill](05-write-your-first-skill.md)

There are two ways to get a skill into a conversation: let the agent choose, or force it. Most of the time you should let it choose — but knowing the manual path makes debugging trivial.

---

## Way 1 · Just describe the task (recommended)

OpenCode advertises every eligible skill at each step. Describe what you want and the matching skill is loaded automatically.

```text
Review my staged changes and write a commit message.
```

The agent compares your request to descriptions like *"Use when writing, reviewing, or fixing git commit messages"* and loads `commit-message-writer` before answering.

**Good prompts name the artifact:**

| Prompt | Likely to trigger |
| --- | --- |
| "Turn this CSV into a formatted spreadsheet." | `xlsx` |
| "The API returns 429s under load." | `rate-limiting`, `caching-strategies` |
| "Write release notes for v2.3.0." | `git-commits`, `changelog-writing` |

**Weak prompts leave the match to chance:**

| Prompt | Problem |
| --- | --- |
| "Help me with this." | no artifact, no action |
| "Do the thing from yesterday." | no shared context |
| "Make it better." | nothing to match against |

## Way 2 · Force it with `@skill-id`

Mention the ID and OpenCode loads that skill regardless of description matching:

```text
@hello-skill show me what you do
@pdf-handling extract the tables from invoice.pdf into markdown
```

Rules that trip people up:

- Use the **path-derived ID**, not the frontmatter `name`.
- IDs are **case-sensitive**.
- No `.md`, no folder path, no `@skills/`.

| Installed at | Correct invocation |
| --- | --- |
| `.opencode/skills/git-release/SKILL.md` | `@git-release` |
| `.opencode/skills/teams/release/SKILL.md` | `@release` |
| `.opencode/skills/Review.md` | `@Review` |
| `.opencode/skills/git-release/SKILL.md` (`name: Git Release`) | `@git-release` ← not `@Git Release` |

## How to verify it actually loaded

Ask questions only the file can answer:

```text
Load hello-skill, then tell me:
1. The absolute path of the SKILL.md you read.
2. The exact wording of step 2 in the workflow.
```

If the answer matches the file byte-for-byte, it loaded. If it paraphrases something plausible but different, the model is guessing — your skill did not load.

Practical checks, in order:

1. New session? (Discovery happens at session start.)
2. `description` present in the frontmatter?
3. Filename exactly `SKILL.md`?
4. ID spelled exactly, with the right case?
5. Is another source shadowing the same ID?

## Keep loaded skills from becoming noise

Skills stay in the conversation once loaded. If a long session drifts, start fresh rather than piling on more instructions.

For skills you want **available but never automatic** — think "dangerous deploy helper" — set:

```yaml
metadata:
  opencode/autoinvoke: false
```

The agent no longer sees it in the list, but `@deploy-prod` still works. That is exactly the behavior you want for anything with side effects.

## Control who can load what

Permissions use `action: "skill"` and the skill ID as the resource. Rules run in order; the last match wins.

```jsonc
// opencode.json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "skill", "resource": "*",            "effect": "allow" },
    { "action": "skill", "resource": "internal-*",   "effect": "deny"  },
    { "action": "skill", "resource": "deploy-*",     "effect": "ask"   }
  ]
}
```

| Effect | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `allow` | Advertised and loaded without asking |
| `ask` | Advertised, but you approve each load |
| `deny` | Hidden from the model and impossible to load |

Scope the same rules to one agent by putting them under `agents.<id>.permissions`.

## A worked session

```text
you  ›  My staged diff adds a retry wrapper. Write the commit message.

     · skill commit-message-writer loaded
     · running: git diff --staged

ai   › feat(http): retry idempotent requests on 429

       Adds exponential backoff for GET/PUT with a 3-attempt cap.
       Commit this message? [y/N]
```

Note what made it work: the request named a real action ("write the commit message") that the description promises.

---

## Check yourself

1. You installed `pr-review-checklist` and typed `@PR Review Checklist`. Why does it fail?
2. What is the difference between `deny` and `opencode/autoinvoke: false`?
3. Your skill loads but the agent ignores its steps. What is the most likely cause?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The ID is `pr-review-checklist` — path-derived, lowercase kebab-case, case-sensitive.
2. `deny` blocks loading entirely. `autoinvoke: false` hides it from automatic discovery but still allows explicit `@id` loading.
3. The body is vague. Models follow concrete, numbered steps and explicit rules far more reliably than prose like "be careful and use good judgment".
</details>

# 05 · Write your first skill

> **Time:** 20 minutes · **Prev:** [04 · Use a skill](04-use-a-skill.md) · **Next:** [06 · Global vs. project](06-global-vs-project.md)

You already installed one. Now write one you will keep. We will build a commit-message skill, but the structure applies to anything: deploy checklists, review procedures, document formats, data pipelines, incident runbooks.

---

## Step 1 · Pick a workflow you repeat

Good first skills are **narrow, checkable, and frequent**:

- ✅ "Write commit messages in Conventional Commits format."
- ✅ "Summarize a PR diff into reviewer-friendly bullets."
- ✅ "Convert a CSV into a formatted .xlsx with a summary sheet."
- ❌ "Be a better engineer." (not a procedure)
- ❌ "Handle all my documents." (no boundary)

Write down the one sentence you are tired of repeating. That sentence becomes the skill.

## Step 2 · Create the folder

```bash
mkdir -p .opencode/skills/commit-message-writer/references
```

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force .opencode\skills\commit-message-writer\references
```

Directory form is strongly preferred over a flat `commit-message-writer.md`, because supporting files get a private base directory:

```text
commit-message-writer/
├── SKILL.md
└── references/
    └── conventional-commits.md
```

## Step 3 · Write frontmatter

```markdown
---
name: Commit Message Writer
description: Use when writing, reviewing, or fixing a git commit message or pull request description
---
```

### The `description` is 90% of the skill

It is the only thing the model sees before loading. Write it as **"Use when …"** and include the words a user would actually type.

| ❌ Doesn't trigger | ✅ Triggers |
| --- | --- |
| `description: Git helper` | `description: Use when writing, reviewing, or fixing a git commit message or PR description` |
| `description: Excel stuff` | `description: Use when creating, editing, or analyzing .xlsx spreadsheets, formulas, or pivot tables` |
| `description: Helps with security` | `description: Use when auditing code for SQL injection, XSS, auth bypass, or secret leakage` |

Checklist for a description:

- Starts with a verb phrase or "Use when…"
- Names the **artifact** (commit message, .xlsx, SQL schema)
- Names the **situation** (before committing, during review, under load)
- Stays roughly under 200 characters
- Does not overlap with a skill you already have

### Optional switches

```yaml
metadata:
  opencode/autoinvoke: false   # hide from auto-discovery, keep @id working
```

Use this for anything destructive: deploys, migrations, bulk deletions, expense approvals.

## Step 4 · Write the body

A body that models follow has five parts. Not every skill needs all five, but the order is reliable.

```markdown
# Commit Message Writer

## When to use
The user asks for a commit message, or a commit is about to be created.

## Inputs
- The staged diff (`git diff --staged`)
- Optional: the issue or ticket ID

## Workflow
1. Run `git diff --staged` and read the whole change. If the diff is empty, stop and say so.
2. Classify the change: feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, chore, perf, build, ci.
3. Choose a scope from the changed paths — `auth`, `api`, `ui`. Never invent one.
4. Draft `<type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>` in 72 characters or less.
5. If the body needs detail, add a blank line and wrap at 72 columns.
6. Show the message. Wait for approval. Only then run `git commit`.

## Rules
- Imperative mood: "add", not "added" or "adds".
- One logical change per commit. If the diff mixes unrelated work, say so instead of hiding it.
- Never claim a ticket reference the user did not provide.

## Examples
Input: adds retry with backoff to GET/PUT
Output: `feat(http): retry idempotent requests on 429`

Input: fixes null crash in avatar upload
Output: `fix(upload): guard against missing filename`
```

### Why this shape works

| Section | Job |
| --- | --- |
| **When to use** | Disambiguates from neighboring skills |
| **Inputs** | Stops the agent from inventing data |
| **Workflow** | Numbered steps the model can follow and you can audit |
| **Rules** | Constraints, including hard stops |
| **Examples** | Shows the target format better than prose can |

### Writing rules that actually constrain behavior

| Weak | Strong |
| --- | --- |
| "Be concise." | "Keep the subject line ≤ 72 characters." |
| "Use good judgment." | "If the diff touches more than one module, stop and ask which change to commit first." |
| "Don't make mistakes." | "If `git diff --staged` returns nothing, report that and stop." |
| "Follow best practices." | "Reference `references/conventional-commits.md` for allowed types." |

Explicit stop conditions are the highest-value lines in any skill. They are what turns a suggestion into a procedure.

## Step 5 · Add supporting files (optional)

Keep the body short; push reference material into files the body points at:

```markdown
## Reference
Read `references/conventional-commits.md` before choosing a type.
```

Paths inside a skill are **relative to the folder containing `SKILL.md`**. The agent receives that base directory plus a sample of up to ten supporting file paths — but **it does not read them until the body tells it to**.

That is the right place for long lookup tables, style guides, templates, and schemas. It is the wrong place for critical instructions, because a model under time pressure may skip a file it was not explicitly told to open.

## Step 6 · Test it like a user

Start a **new** session, then try three prompts:

```text
1. @commit-message-writer write a message for my staged changes
2. Write a commit message for my staged changes.        ← does it auto-trigger?
3. What does the commit-message-writer skill require before committing?   ← did the rules land?
```

Then test the boundaries:

```text
4. Write a commit message for an empty diff.            ← should stop, not hallucinate
5. Commit this and push to main.                        ← should ask, not act
```

If (2) fails but (1) works, your description is too vague. If (5) acts without asking, your rules are too soft.

## Step 7 · Version it

Skills are code. Keep them in git:

```bash
git add .opencode/skills/commit-message-writer
git commit -m "feat(skills): add commit-message-writer"
```

Two habits that pay off:

- **One skill per commit** — makes `git log` a changelog of your agent's behavior.
- **Bump a `version` in frontmatter** if you serve the skill from an HTTP catalog, since caches key off it.

## Step 8 · Prune

Re-read every skill monthly and ask: *did this fire in the last 30 days?* Skills that never fire are not free — they add description noise that makes real matches less certain. Delete the folder and move on.

---

## Common failure modes

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Never auto-triggers | Vague description | Add the artifact and situation words |
| Triggers constantly | Description too broad | Narrow it; add "Use **only** when…" |
| Triggers on everything | Two overlapping skills | Merge them or sharpen the boundary |
| Steps skipped | Body is prose, not a list | Numbered workflow + explicit rules |
| Reads the wrong file | Absolute or `../` paths | Use paths relative to `SKILL.md` |
| Different result each run | Ambiguous inputs | Add an **Inputs** section and stop conditions |
| Works locally, not for teammate | Installed globally | Move it into `.opencode/skills/` and commit |

---

## Check yourself

1. Rewrite this description: `description: Helps with tests`.
2. What belongs in `references/` rather than in the body?
3. Why should a destructive skill set `opencode/autoinvoke: false`?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Example: `Use when writing, fixing, or reviewing unit, integration, or end-to-end tests, including flaky test triage`.
2. Long lookup material (style guides, schemas, type tables) that is only needed for part of the workflow — while critical instructions stay in the body.
3. So it never loads by accident. The model cannot see it; you must type `@skill-id` deliberately.
</details>

# 08 · Skills vs. agents vs. commands

> **Time:** 6 minutes · **Prev:** [07 · Load from a URL](07-load-from-url.md) · **Next:** [09 · Troubleshooting](09-troubleshooting.md)

OpenCode gives you several ways to shape agent behavior. They overlap just enough to be confusing. Here is the short version.

---

## The one-line distinction

| Primitive | Who starts it | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Skill** | the **model**, when a task matches | a procedure the agent can load on demand |
| **Agent** | **you**, by selecting it | a role with its own model, tools, and permissions |
| **Command** | **you**, by invoking it | a saved prompt, run deliberately |
| **MCP server** | the model, as a tool | external tools and data over a protocol |
| **Plugin** | the runtime | code that extends OpenCode itself |

## Skills

**A skill is knowledge.** It answers "how do we do this here?" and costs nothing until it is used.

Use a skill when:

- The knowledge is procedural and repeatable ("how we write migrations")
- It should apply across many tasks, not just when you remember
- You want it versioned in the repo with no code
- Multiple agents should be able to reuse it

```text
.opencode/skills/migrations/SKILL.md
```

## Agents

**An agent is a role.** It bundles a persona, a model, a tool allowlist, and permissions. Switching agents can change *what the assistant is allowed to do*, not just what it knows.

Use an agent when:

- You want a cheap/fast model for one kind of work and a strong model for another
- You need a restricted toolset (read-only reviewer, no-bash planner)
- You want a different system prompt entirely

A skill can be loaded *by* an agent. An agent is not a substitute for a skill, and vice versa.

> Configuration details for agents live in the official docs: <https://opencode.ai/docs/agents/>

## Commands

**A command is a prompt with a name.** You type it; it runs. Nothing decides for you.

Use a command when:

- The action is explicit and intentional ("deploy staging")
- It takes arguments you want to supply each time
- You do not want the model choosing it on its own

If you find yourself typing the same prompt daily, a command removes the typing. If you find the model *should* have known to do it, that is a skill.

## Side-by-side

| Question | Skill | Agent | Command |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Can the model trigger it unprompted? | ✅ yes | — | ❌ no |
| Can it change the model? | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Can it restrict tools? | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Is it just Markdown? | ✅ | mostly | ✅ |
| Should it live in the repo? | ✅ often | sometimes | ✅ often |
| Good for "how we do X"? | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Good for "only read, never write"? | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |

## Practical combinations

**Reviewer skill + review agent.** The skill holds your review checklist; a read-only agent holds the permission boundary.

**Deploy command + deploy skill.** The command is the deliberate trigger; the skill holds the runbook steps so the prompt stays short.

**Global code-review skill.** Every project gets the same baseline, and each repo can override it with a project-scoped skill of the same ID.

## What about MCP and plugins?

| You want… | Reach for |
| --- | --- |
| To teach a procedure in Markdown | **Skill** |
| To query Jira/Postgres/Linear live | **MCP server** |
| To add a new tool or hook to OpenCode | **Plugin** |
| To pin a model and toolset | **Agent** |
| To save a prompt you repeat | **Command** |

A common beginner mistake is reaching for an MCP server to encode a workflow. If no live data is involved, a skill is lighter, safer, and reviewable in a diff.

---

## Check yourself

1. You want "always run the linter before committing". Skill or agent?
2. You want a reviewer that physically cannot edit files. Skill or agent?
3. You want a one-shot `/release 1.4.0`. Skill, agent, or command?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Skill — it is a procedure the model should apply on its own.
2. Agent — the restriction is a permission boundary, not knowledge. Pair it with a review skill.
3. Command, ideally backed by a release skill that holds the steps.
</details>

# Commit Message Writer

Turns a staged diff into a commit message that still makes sense in six months.

## When to use

- The user asks for a commit message or a PR title/description
- A commit is about to be created and no message has been agreed
- An existing message needs review ("is this a good message?")

## Inputs

- The staged diff: `git diff --staged`
- Optional: a ticket or issue ID the user supplied

If the diff is empty, fall back to `git diff` and say which one you read. If both are empty, stop — do not invent a change.

## Workflow

1. Run `git diff --staged` and read the entire change.
2. Classify it using `references/conventional-commits.md`: feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, chore, perf, build, ci.
3. Choose a scope from the **changed paths only** — for example `auth`, `api`, `ui`, `deps`.
4. Draft `<type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>`, 72 characters or fewer.
5. If more context is needed, add a blank line, then a body wrapped at 72 columns explaining **why**, not what.
6. Show the message and wait for approval. Only then run `git commit -m "…"`.

## Rules

- Imperative mood: "add retry", never "added" or "adds".
- One logical change per commit. If the diff mixes unrelated work, say so and propose a split instead of hiding it.
- Never invent a ticket reference, co-author, or issue number.
- Never add tool attribution or "Generated with" footers.
- Do not push, amend, or rewrite history unless explicitly asked.
- Never mention that you are following a skill in the commit message itself.

## Examples

```text
Input: retry with exponential backoff for GET/PUT
Output: feat(http): retry idempotent requests on 429

Input: null crash when an avatar upload has no filename
Output: fix(upload): guard against missing filename

Input: reorder imports in three files
Output: chore(lint): sort imports in auth module
```

Breaking change:

```text
feat(api)!: require auth on /v2/search

Removes the anonymous fallback that returned 403s after the
rate-limit change. Clients must send a bearer token.
```

## Output format

Reply with the message in one fenced block, then a single line asking whether to commit. Nothing else.

# PR Review Checklist

A review that finds the bug CI cannot see: the one in the logic.

## When to use

- The user asks for a review of a diff, branch, or PR
- A merge is being considered
- A change touches auth, money, data deletion, or migrations

## Inputs

- The diff: `git diff <base>...HEAD` or the PR's changed files
- The repo's test and lint commands, if discoverable
- Any stated intent from the author

If you cannot see the diff, ask for it. Do not review from the description alone.

## Workflow

1. **Read the stated intent.** One sentence: what is this supposed to change?
2. **Read the diff in file order.** Note files that are unrelated to the intent.
3. **Check correctness.** Off-by-one, empty inputs, null/undefined, error paths, retries, timeouts.
4. **Check boundaries.** Authn/authz on every new path, tenant isolation, input validation, output encoding.
5. **Check data.** Migrations reversible? Backfill safe on a live table? Deletes scoped?
6. **Check tests.** Do they assert behavior, or just execute lines? Is the failure case covered?
7. **Check blast radius.** Feature flag? Rollback path? Logging that would leak secrets?
8. **Report findings ordered by severity**, each with file:line and a concrete fix.

## Rules

- Cite `file:line` for every finding. No vague "consider improving error handling".
- Separate **blocking** issues from **nice-to-have** suggestions.
- If the diff is too large to review well, say so and propose a split before continuing.
- Never approve a change you could not read in full.
- Do not restate the diff back to the author. They wrote it.
- If nothing is wrong, say so plainly and name the two things you verified.
- Read `references/severity-guide.md` before assigning severity.

## Output format

```markdown
## Verdict
<approve | approve with nits | request changes>

## Blocking
1. `src/auth/session.ts:42` — refresh token accepted after rotation. Fix: compare `token_version` before issuing.

## Non-blocking
- `src/ui/Button.tsx:12` — prop name `onClickk` typo.

## Verified
- Auth middleware applied to both new routes.
- Migration has a working `down()`.
```

## Stop conditions

Stop and ask, rather than guessing, when:

- The diff includes generated files or lockfiles you cannot interpret
- The change requires domain knowledge not present in the repo
- You would need to run destructive commands to verify behavior

One page. Print it, pin it, ignore the rest of the repo until you need it.

## The shape of a skill

```text
.opencode/skills/<id>/
├── SKILL.md
└── references/        ← optional
```

```markdown
---
name: Display Name
description: Use when <situation> and <artifact> are involved
---

## Workflow
1. …

```

## Where things go

| Scope | Path |
| --- | --- |
| Global | `~/.config/opencode/skills/<id>/SKILL.md` |
| Project | `.opencode/skills/<id>/SKILL.md` |
| Claude compat | `~/.claude/skills/`, `.claude/skills/` |
| Agents compat | `~/.agents/skills/`, `.agents/skills/` |

## Three commands

```bash

curl -fsSL https://opencodeskills.dev/install.sh | sh -s -- install --project git-commits

```

## Invoke

```text
Write me a commit message for the staged diff.     ← auto, description match
@commit-message-writer write the commit message     ← explicit, always works
```

- Use the **path-derived ID**, not the frontmatter name
- IDs are **case-sensitive**
- Start a **new session** after creating or installing a skill

## Frontmatter

```yaml
name: Commit Message Writer
description: Use when writing, reviewing, or fixing git commit messages
metadata:
  opencode/autoinvoke: false    # optional: hide from auto-discovery
```

| Field | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | Display label only |
| `description` | Controls auto-discovery — required for triggers |
| `metadata.opencode/autoinvoke: false` | Hidden from the model, still `@id`-loadable |
| `disable-model-invocation: true` | Alias for the above |

## Precedence (lowest → highest)

```text
built-ins → .claude → .agents → ~/.config/opencode → .opencode → opencode.json skills
```

Same ID in two places? The later one wins.

## Description patterns

```yaml

✅ description: Use when creating, editing, or analyzing .xlsx spreadsheets
✅ description: Use only when the user asks to deploy to production
```

# 06 · Global vs. project skills

> **Time:** 8 minutes · **Prev:** [05 · Write your first skill](05-write-your-first-skill.md) · **Next:** [07 · Load from a URL](07-load-from-url.md)

Two folders, one question: **who needs this?**

| | Global | Project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Path | `~/.config/opencode/skills/` | `.opencode/skills/` |
| Visible in | every project on your machine | that repository only |
| Travels with git | no | yes |
| Good for | personal workflow, formatting taste, languages you use everywhere | repo commands, deploy steps, team conventions, domain rules |
| Reviewed by | you | your team, in PRs |

Rules of thumb:

- **Personal habit → global.** "I like Conventional Commits."
- **Repo fact → project.** "Our tests run with `pnpm test:unit`, and staging deploys from `main` only."
- **Anything with credentials or environment names → project, and never commit secrets into it.**

If a project skill and a global skill do the same job, the **project one wins**. That is how you let a repo override your personal default without renaming anything.

---

## Precedence, lowest to highest

```text
1. built-in skills
2. ~/.claude/skills, then .claude/skills (ancestor → current dir)
3. ~/.agents/skills, then .agents/skills (ancestor → current dir)
4. ~/.config/opencode/skills
5. .opencode/skills (project root → current dir)
6. explicit `skills` entries in opencode.json (in config order)
```

Skills are selected **by ID**. If two sources define `git-release`, the later source in that list supplies the version OpenCode loads.

```text
~/.config/opencode/skills/git-release/SKILL.md   ← lower precedence
.opencode/skills/git-release/SKILL.md            ← this one loads
```

> [!TIP]
> Precedence is a feature, not a trap. Keep a generic `code-review` global, then let each repo drop in its own `.opencode/skills/code-review/SKILL.md` for repo-specific rules. Same ID, better answer in that repo.

## Discovery details worth knowing

OpenCode searches **upward from your current directory to the project root** and collects matching skill folders at every level:

```text
repo/
├── .opencode/skills/format/SKILL.md          ← found from anywhere in repo
└── services/api/
    ├── .opencode/skills/api-tests/SKILL.md   ← found from services/api downward
    └── src/                                  ← you are here
```

Inside a source folder:

- Every folder containing `SKILL.md` is **one** skill. OpenCode does not search **inside** it for more skills.
- Flat `*.md` files are only picked up at the **source root**, not in subfolders.
- Hidden folders and `node_modules` are skipped.
- Search stops **six directories** below the source root.
- A skill directory named `skills` inside another skill is not discovered.

## Compatible locations

Skills written for other agents work unchanged:

```text
~/.claude/skills/     ~/.agents/skills/
.claude/skills/       .agents/skills/
```

That means the install path you may already have for Claude Code is live in OpenCode too — no migration, no conversion. OpenCode's own docs list these as global and project "compatibility" sources.

## When to prefer global

- A language or framework you use in every repo
- Personal writing and commit style
- Editor/terminal workflows
- Skills you are still experimenting with

Downside: invisible to teammates, and it silently changes every project. If a global skill changes how a shared repo behaves, it should probably be a project skill instead.

## When to prefer project

- Build, test, lint, and deploy commands for one repo
- Architecture rules ("never import `services/` from `components/`")
- Domain vocabulary (what "account", "tenant", or "shipment" means here)
- Anything reviewed in a pull request
- Anything onboarding a new teammate would need

Upside: discoverable, reviewable, diffable. A new contributor gets your agent behavior on clone.

## Sharing with your team

```text
repo/
└── .opencode/
    └── skills/
        ├── api-tests/
        │   ├── SKILL.md
        │   └── references/
        │       └── fixtures.md
        └── release/
            └── SKILL.md
```

Commit the folder. Teammates need no install step. Treat changes like code:

- One skill per PR, with the motivation in the description.
- Test after editing — start a new session and invoke it.
- Review descriptions, not just bodies; descriptions decide when the skill fires.

## Pin behavior with `opencode.json`

If you want to guarantee a shared set of skills regardless of local folders, commit a config that adds explicit sources:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "skills": ["./team-skills"]
}
```

Relative paths resolve from the **active working directory**, not the config file's location. `~/` expands to your home directory; absolute paths are used as written.

Explicit `skills` entries have the **highest** precedence and are combined across every config file — they are not replaced by a later file.

# 07 · Load skills from a URL (OpenCode 2)

> **Time:** 10 minutes · **Prev:** [06 · Global vs. project](06-global-vs-project.md) · **Next:** [08 · Skills vs. agents vs. commands](08-skills-vs-agents-vs-commands.md)

Instead of copying folders, you can point OpenCode at an **HTTP catalog**. It fetches an `index.json`, advertises those skills to the model, and downloads files only when a skill loads. Nothing lands in your skills folder.

Requires **OpenCode 2**.

---

## Use an existing catalog

Add URLs to the `skills` array of `opencode.json` — global at `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`, or per-repo at the project root:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "skills": [
    "https://opencodeskills.dev/catalog/",
    "https://opencodeskills.dev/catalog/documentation/",
    "https://opencodeskills.dev/catalog/testing/"
  ]
}
```

Then **start a new session**. The catalog's skills now appear beside your local ones.

Trade-offs to weigh before you add the whole directory:

| | Catalog URL | Local folders |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Disk footprint | zero | full copies |
| Updates | automatic | you reinstall |
| Works offline | no | yes |
| Auditable before use | not really | yes — you can read the file |
| Survives a dead URL | no | yes |

> [!WARNING]
> A catalog is **remote instructions** that your agent will follow. Prefer catalogs you trust, and review a skill before you rely on it for anything with side effects. For security-sensitive repos, install locally so the content is in the diff.

## How the protocol works

A catalog is a base URL serving `index.json`:

```json
{
  "skills": [
    {
      "name": "git-release",
      "version": "3",
      "files": ["git-release.md", "references/release-policy.md"]
    },
    {
      "name": "pdf-handling",
      "version": "1",
      "files": ["SKILL.md", "references/forms.md"]
    }
  ]
}
```

For each entry, OpenCode downloads `<base-url>/<name>/<file>`.

| Rule | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Paths | Safe, relative, same-origin |
| Entry file | Include `SKILL.md` **or** `<name>.md` |
| Updates | Increment `version` when files change, or the cache will not refresh |

Each downloaded directory becomes a source root named after the entry, so both `git-release.md` and `SKILL.md` resolve to the ID `git-release`.

## Publish your own catalog

Any static host works — S3, Cloudflare R2, GitHub Pages, a bucket behind a CDN. You need:

```text
https://example.com/skills/
├── index.json
├── commit-message-writer/
│   ├── SKILL.md
│   └── references/
│       └── conventional-commits.md
└── pdf-handling/
    └── SKILL.md
```

```json
{
  "skills": [
    {
      "name": "commit-message-writer",
      "version": "1",
      "files": ["SKILL.md", "references/conventional-commits.md"]
    },
    {
      "name": "pdf-handling",
      "version": "1",
      "files": ["SKILL.md"]
    }
  ]
}
```

Checklist before you share the URL:

- `index.json` is served with `Content-Type: application/json`
- Every listed file exists at the exact path
- All listed paths are same-origin and contain no `..`
- `version` is incremented on every content change
- Private skills are **not** in a public catalog

Then teammates add one line:

```jsonc
{ "skills": ["https://example.com/skills/"] }
```

## Mixing catalogs and folders

All `skills` entries are combined. Local paths, `~/` paths, absolute paths, and URLs can coexist:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "skills": [
    "./team-skills",
    "~/shared/opencode-skills",
    "/opt/company-skills",
    "https://opencodeskills.dev/catalog/documentation/"
  ]
}
```

Explicit entries take precedence over discovered folders, in array order.

## Debugging a catalog

| Symptom | Check |
| --- | --- |
| No skills appear | Is the host OpenCode 2? Does `<base>/index.json` return valid JSON? |
| Some entries missing | Does every listed file return 200? |
| Skill loads stale content | Bump `version` in `index.json` |
| 403 / CORS errors | Serve from the same origin as the catalog base URL; allow GET |
| Wrong content loads | Same ID defined in a higher-precedence local folder |

# 09 · Troubleshooting

> **Prev:** [08 · Skills vs. agents vs. commands](08-skills-vs-agents-vs-commands.md) · **Next:** [10 · Glossary](10-glossary.md)

Work top to bottom. These six causes account for nearly every "my skill is not loading".

---

## The six-cause checklist

### 1. Filename is wrong

Only two names count:

- a **root-level** `*.md` file inside a source folder, e.g. `skills/review.md`
- a file named **exactly** `SKILL.md`, e.g. `skills/git-release/SKILL.md`

```text
✅ skills/git-release/SKILL.md
❌ skills/git-release/skill.md
❌ skills/git-release/SKILL.MD
❌ skills/git-release/README.md
```

Case matters on Linux and macOS.

### 2. The folder is nested wrong

```text
❌ ~/.config/opencode/skills/xlsx/xlsx/SKILL.md
✅ ~/.config/opencode/skills/xlsx/SKILL.md
```

Also check that you are not inside another skill's folder — OpenCode does not search inside a skill directory for more skills:

```text
❌ .opencode/skills/git-release/extras/notes/SKILL.md
```

### 3. The session is stale

Discovery happens **at session start**. A folder created mid-session will not appear. Start a new session in the directory where the skill should be visible.

### 4. No `description`

A skill without a `description` is never advertised to the model. It still exists, and `@id` can load it, but auto-invocation is impossible.

```markdown
---
name: Release Helper
description: Use when preparing a release, writing release notes, or bumping a version
---
```

### 5. The ID is wrong

The ID is derived from the path, not the `name` field, and it is **case-sensitive**.

| Installed | ID |
| --- | --- |
| `.opencode/skills/git-release/SKILL.md` | `git-release` |
| `.opencode/skills/teams/release/SKILL.md` | `release` |
| `.opencode/skills/Review.md` | `Review` |
| `name: Git Release` in the frontmatter | *still not an ID* |

For portable skills use lowercase kebab-case and match the folder name: `^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$`.

### 6. Something is overriding it

Skills resolve by ID, and later sources win:

```text
built-in → .claude/ → .agents/ → ~/.config/opencode/ → .opencode/ → opencode.json `skills`
```

Find the duplicate:

```bash
find . ~/.config/opencode ~/.claude ~/.agents -name SKILL.md 2>/dev/null | sort
```

```powershell
Get-ChildItem -Path .,"$HOME\.config\opencode","$HOME\.claude","$HOME\.agents" -Recurse -Filter SKILL.md -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object -ExpandProperty FullName
```

---

## Symptom → cause table

| Symptom | Most likely cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Skill never triggers | Missing/narrow `description` | Rewrite as "Use when …" with artifact words |
| `@name` does nothing | Wrong ID or case | Use the path-derived ID exactly |
| Two skills fight | Overlapping descriptions | Merge, or scope with "Use **only** when…" |
| Loads, then ignores steps | Prose body | Numbered workflow + explicit rules |
| Reads a reference file that does not exist | Wrong relative path | Paths are relative to the `SKILL.md` folder |
| Works for you, not a teammate | Installed globally | Move into `.opencode/skills/` and commit |
| Worked yesterday, not today | Another source now defines the ID | Check precedence |
| Catalog skills missing | `index.json`, same-origin, or `version` | Validate JSON; bump `version` |
| Model sees nothing at all | Permissions deny | Check `action: "skill"` rules |
| Hidden from the model but `@id` works | `opencode/autoinvoke: false` | Intended behavior |

---

## Fast diagnostics

**Is the file where you think it is?**

```bash
ls -l .opencode/skills/*/SKILL.md
```

```powershell
Get-ChildItem .opencode\skills\*\SKILL.md
```

**Does the frontmatter parse?**

```bash
node scripts/validate-skills.mjs
```

The script in this repo checks for `SKILL.md`, a `name`, a `description`, and a valid kebab-case folder ID.

**Did permissions block it?**

```jsonc
{
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "skill", "resource": "*", "effect": "allow" }
  ]
}
```

Rules are evaluated in order and the **last** match wins, so a broad `deny` at the end beats an `allow` above it.

**Is it a catalog problem?**

Open `https://<base>/index.json` in a browser. If it does not render as JSON, the catalog is the problem — not your config.

---

## Still stuck? Reduce to one variable

1. Delete every skill except the one you are debugging.
2. Put it in `.opencode/skills/` inside a **new empty folder**.
3. `cd` into that folder.
4. Start a session there and run `@that-skill-id`.
5. Confirm the file path the model reports.

If that works, the skill is fine and the problem is scope, precedence, or permissions. If it fails, the problem is the file itself — usually the name, the depth, or the frontmatter.

---

## Reporting a bug in a skill

Include:

- The exact install path
- The frontmatter block
- The prompt you used
- Whether `@id` works
- The version from `opencode --version`

That is usually enough to reproduce it in one pass.

# 10 · Glossary

> **Prev:** [09 · Troubleshooting](09-troubleshooting.md) · **Home:** [README](../README.md)

Terms used throughout this repo, in the order you are likely to meet them.

---

**Agent** — A role with its own system prompt, model, tools, and permissions. You select an agent; a skill is loaded in addition to it. See [08](08-skills-vs-agents-vs-commands.md).

**Advertise** — Showing the model the list of skill IDs, names, and descriptions at each step. No body text is included. Skills without a description are not advertised.

**Base directory** — The folder containing `SKILL.md`. Relative paths inside the skill resolve here, and the model receives it plus a sample of up to ten supporting file paths when the skill loads.

**Catalog (HTTP)** — A base URL serving `index.json`, listing skills, versions, and files. Added to the `skills` array in `opencode.json`. OpenCode 2 only. See [07](07-load-from-url.md).

**Command** — A saved prompt you invoke by name. The model cannot trigger it on its own.

**Compatibility sources** — Locations used by other agents that OpenCode also reads: `~/.claude/skills/`, `~/.agents/skills/`, and their project equivalents.

**`description`** — The frontmatter field that decides when a skill is offered to the model. The single highest-leverage line in a skill.

**Directory form** — A skill stored as `skills/<id>/SKILL.md`. Recommended, because supporting files sit beside the entry file.

**Discovery** — The scan OpenCode performs when a session starts, walking the known source folders.

**Flat form** — A skill stored as a root-level `skills/<id>.md` file. Valid, but it cannot ship supporting files as cleanly.

**Frontmatter** — The YAML block between `---` lines at the top of `SKILL.md`. `name`, `description`, `metadata`, and `disable-model-invocation` are interpreted.

**Global scope** — `~/.config/opencode/skills/`. Available in every project on your machine.

**ID** — The identifier used to load a skill, derived from its path. Case-sensitive. `skills/git-release/SKILL.md` → `git-release`.

**`index.json`** — The manifest at a catalog's base URL. Lists `name`, `version`, and `files` per skill. Bump `version` to bust the cache.

**kebab-case** — `lowercase-words-with-hyphens`. The recommended ID shape: `^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$`.

**Load** — Actually pulling a skill's Markdown body into the conversation. Happens on a description match or an explicit `@id`.

**`metadata.opencode/autoinvoke`** — Set to `false` to hide a skill from automatic discovery while keeping `@id` loading available.

**`disable-model-invocation`** — Portability alias for the same behavior. If both are set, `opencode/autoinvoke` wins.

**MCP server** — External tools and data exposed over a protocol. Different from a skill; skills teach procedure, MCP supplies capability.

**`opencode.json` / `opencode.jsonc`** — Configuration file. Its `skills` array adds local folders or HTTP catalogs and has the highest precedence.

**Plugin** — Code that extends OpenCode itself. Unlike a skill, it executes.

**Precedence** — The order sources are consulted when two define the same ID. Later wins: built-ins → `.claude/` → `.agents/` → `~/.config/opencode/` → `.opencode/` → explicit `skills` entries.

**Project scope** — `.opencode/skills/` at the repository root (or in a subdirectory). Shared with everyone who clones the repo.

**Reference file** — Material beside `SKILL.md` in `references/`, read only when the body instructs the agent to open it.

**Shadowing** — When a higher-precedence source supplies a different skill under the same ID, hiding the lower one.

**Skill** — A folder with `SKILL.md` teaching a repeatable workflow, loaded on demand.

**Skill tool** — The tool the model calls with a skill ID to load that skill's body.

**Source root** — A folder OpenCode scans for skills, such as `.opencode/skills/`, a path in the `skills` array, or a downloaded catalog entry.

**Supporting file** — Any file beside `SKILL.md` (scripts, references, templates). Not loaded automatically.

**Trigger** — A user request whose wording matches a skill's `description`, causing the model to load it.

**`@skill-id`** — Explicit invocation in a prompt. Skips description matching.

# Lab 1 · Install and invoke

**Goal:** prove that discovery works before you write anything of your own.
**Time:** 10 minutes.

## Setup

```bash
mkdir -p ~/skill-lab && cd ~/skill-lab
mkdir -p .opencode/skills/hello-skill
```

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "$HOME\skill-lab\.opencode\skills\hello-skill"
Set-Location "$HOME\skill-lab"
```

Copy [`../examples/hello-skill/SKILL.md`](../examples/hello-skill/SKILL.md) into that folder.

## Tasks

1. Start a new OpenCode session in `~/skill-lab`.
2. Ask, without using `@`:

   ```text
   Can you demo how skills work for me?
   ```

3. Note whether `hello-skill` loaded on its own.
4. Now force it:

   ```text
   @hello-skill show me what you do
   ```

5. Ask for its path:

   ```text
   Which directory did you load hello-skill from? Give me the absolute path.
   ```

## Success criteria

- [ ] The forced invocation loads the skill
- [ ] The reported path is `~/skill-lab/.opencode/skills/hello-skill`
- [ ] The reply stays under 60 words (the skill's own rule)
- [ ] No files were created

## Observe and record

- Did step 2 trigger it automatically? If not, why not? Compare the prompt's wording to the skill's `description`.
- Change the description to `description: Use when the user asks anything at all` and repeat step 2. What happens? Revert it.
- What happens if you delete `description` entirely and repeat step 2? Repeat step 4?

## Cleanup

Leave the folder. Lab 3 reuses this habit of starting from a known-good state.

# Solutions

Read only after attempting the lab.

---

## Lab 1

**Auto-trigger behavior.** "Can you demo how skills work for me?" is a plausible match — the description includes "a demo of how skills work" — so it may load on its own. Whether it does on the first try is less important than what you learned: the description is what did the matching.

**Overbroad description.** Changing it to `Use when the user asks anything at all` makes the skill fire on nearly every request, including unrelated ones. That is the failure mode behind "why does my agent keep doing X?" — the description is too greedy.

**Deleting `description`.** Auto-invocation stops completely; the skill is no longer advertised. `@hello-skill` still works, because explicit loading does not need a description. That is the cleanest demonstration of advertise-vs-load in the whole repo.

## Lab 2

There is no single right skill, so grade against behavior, not prose:

| Criterion | What "good" looks like |
| --- | --- |
| Trigger | Prompt 2 loads it without `@` |
| Precision | It does **not** fire on "write a commit message" |
| Workflow | Numbered, each step checkable |
| Stop condition | Empty input produces a refusal, not invented content |
| Side effects | Destructive request produces a question, not an action |
| Reference | The file exists, and the body says **when** to read it |

Two common near-misses:

1. **Rule bloat.** Ten rules that all say "be careful" teach nothing. Two hard constraints beat ten soft ones.
2. **Reference without instruction.** Adding `references/style.md` without a line like *"Read `references/style.md` before choosing headings"* means the model may never open it — supporting files are not loaded automatically.

## Lab 3

The fixture has **six** defects. Five are real; one is intentional ambiguity.

### 1. Wrong filename — blocker

```text
labs/fixtures/broken-skill/skill.md      ❌
labs/fixtures/broken-skill/SKILL.md      ✅
```

Discovery only accepts a root-level `*.md` or a file named exactly `SKILL.md`. On Linux and macOS the case mismatch is fatal. This is why `@xlsx` does nothing at all: the skill was never registered.

Running the validator makes it obvious:

```text
No SKILL.md files found. Point the script at a folder that contains skills.
```

### 2. Missing `description` — blocker for auto-discovery

```yaml
---
name: Excel Helper
---
```

Even after the rename, the skill loads only via `@xlsx`. The model never sees it in the available list. Fix:

```yaml
description: Use when creating, editing, or analyzing .xlsx spreadsheets, formulas, or pivot tables
```

### 3. Dangling reference — error

The body says *"follow `references/formulas.md`"*, but that file does not exist. The validator catches it:

```text
references missing file `references/formulas.md`
```

Either create the file or remove the line. A dangling reference is worse than none: the model will either hallucinate the file's contents or stall.

### 4. Folder/ID mismatch — warning

The lab copies the fixture to `xlsx`, so the ID becomes `xlsx` while the frontmatter `name` is `Excel Helper`. That is legal, but confusing — the `name` is a label, the path is the identity. Best practice: folder, ID, and a lowercase-kebab `name` line up.

### 5. Useless body — quality defect

```markdown
1. Ask the user what they want to do.
2. Open the file.
```

No inputs, no rules, no output format. This skill cannot produce a consistent result. The fixed version needs a workflow with real steps and an explicit output shape.

### 6. Missing scope guidance — the ambiguous one

Nothing says when **not** to use it. A reader cannot tell whether this skill covers CSVs, Google Sheets, or Excel macros. Add a boundary:

```markdown
## When not to use
- CSV-only work (no formulas or formatting)
- Google Sheets
```

## The fixed version

```markdown
---
name: xlsx
description: Use when creating, editing, or analyzing .xlsx spreadsheets, formulas, or pivot tables
---

# xlsx

## When to use
The user wants to create, edit, or analyze an Excel workbook.

## When not to use
CSV-only work, Google Sheets, or macro/VBA projects.

## Inputs
- The workbook path, or the data to write
- The sheet name, if the user named one

## Workflow
1. Confirm the file exists before editing. If it does not, ask whether to create it.
2. Read the sheet names and headers before changing anything.
3. When writing formulas, read `references/formulas.md` first.
4. Save to a new file if the original is the only copy.
5. Report which sheet and range changed.

## Rules
- Never overwrite the only copy without asking.
- Never invent a sheet name the user did not mention.
- If the file is not a valid .xlsx, stop and report it.

## Output format
One line: `Updated <sheet>!<range> in <file>.`
```

Validate it:

```bash
node scripts/validate-skills.mjs path/to/xlsx
# ✓ 0 error(s), 0 warning(s)
```

## Bug report format

```text
Path:    ~/skill-lab-3/.opencode/skills/xlsx/skill.md
Symptom: @xlsx does nothing; no skill listed in session
Cause:   Filename is `skill.md`; discovery requires exactly `SKILL.md`
Follow-up: missing `description` would have blocked auto-invocation next
```

That is the whole discipline: **path, symptom, cause, next defect**. It turns "it doesn't work" into something a teammate can act on.

# Conventional Commits — quick reference

Source of truth: <https://www.conventionalcommits.org/>

## Format

```text
<type>[optional scope][!]: <description>

[optional body]

[optional footer(s)]
```

## Types

| Type | Use for | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `feat` | a new user-visible capability | `feat(search): add fuzzy matching` |
| `fix` | a bug fix | `fix(auth): reject expired refresh tokens` |
| `docs` | documentation only | `docs(readme): document the skill install flow` |
| `refactor` | code change with no behavior change | `refactor(parser): extract token scanner` |
| `test` | tests only | `test(api): cover empty-payload 400s` |
| `chore` | maintenance, deps, build config | `chore(deps): bump zod to 4.1.2` |
| `perf` | measurable performance improvement | `perf(query): add covering index for tenant lookups` |
| `build` | build system or packaging | `build(docker): drop dev deps from runtime image` |
| `ci` | CI configuration | `ci: cache pnpm store between jobs` |
| `style` | formatting only, no logic | `style: apply prettier to src/ui` |
| `revert` | reverts a previous commit | `revert: feat(search): add fuzzy matching` |

## Scope

Use the **module, package, or directory** the change touches. One word, lowercase.

```text
feat(checkout): …
fix(upload): …
docs(skills): …
```

Omit the scope when the change spans the whole repo or the type is self-explanatory:

```text
ci: pin Node to 22
```

## Subject line

- Imperative mood — it completes "This commit will…"
- No trailing period
- 72 characters maximum, ideally under 50
- Lowercase after the colon

| ❌ | ✅ |
| --- | --- |
| `Fixed bug` | `fix(parser): handle empty input` |
| `feat: Adds new thing.` | `feat(ui): add dark mode toggle` |
| `update stuff` | `chore(deps): bump esbuild to 0.25.1` |

## Body

Explain **why**, not what — the diff already shows what. Wrap at 72 columns.

```text
fix(auth): reject expired refresh tokens

Tokens issued before the clock-skew fix could pass validation for
up to five minutes past expiry. Rejecting on `exp` closes the gap.
```

## Footers

```text
Refs: PROJ-142
BREAKING CHANGE: `search()` now returns a cursor instead of an offset.
Co-authored-by: Name <email>
```

A `!` after the type or scope also marks a breaking change:

```text
feat(api)!: require auth on /v2/search
```

## Splitting a messy diff

Ask: could any part ship on its own and still leave the repo working? If yes, it is its own commit.

```text
❌ feat(api): add endpoint, fix typo, bump deps, reformat tests
✅ feat(api): add /v2/search endpoint
✅ fix(docs): correct install typo
✅ chore(deps): bump zod to 4.1.2
✅ style(tests): apply prettier to test folder
```

# Severity guide

Use these four levels, and do not inflate them. A review where everything is critical is a review nobody reads.

## Blocker — must fix before merge

The change is wrong, unsafe, or will break production.

- Data loss, corruption, or an unsafe migration on a live table
- Auth bypass, missing authorization check, or cross-tenant leak
- Secrets or credentials committed
- Crash on a realistic input
- Silent failure where the caller believes the operation succeeded
- Breaking change to a public contract with no version bump

```text
src/auth/session.ts:42 — accepts a rotated refresh token (auth bypass)
```

## Major — should fix in this PR

Real defect, limited blast radius, or a trap for the next person.

- Missing error handling on a network or filesystem call
- N+1 query on a hot path
- Test that asserts nothing
- Race condition under concurrent writes
- Unbounded retry or missing timeout

## Minor — fix if cheap

Correct but costly to maintain.

- Duplicated logic that already exists in a helper
- Misleading name (`getUser` that also writes)
- Dead code left behind
- Missing test for an edge case that cannot lose data

## Nit — optional

Style and taste. Say "nit" so the author knows it is not a demand.

- Naming preferences
- Comment wording
- Import order
- Formatting the formatter would fix

## How to phrase a finding

```text
<severity> · <file>:<line> — <what is wrong>. <why it matters>. Fix: <concrete action>.
```

Example:

```text
Major · src/api/search.ts:88 — retry loop has no cap. A 503 storm will
pin a worker indefinitely. Fix: cap at 3 attempts with jittered backoff.
```

## What never belongs in a review

- Restating the diff
- "This could be cleaner" with no target
- Architecture rewrites disguised as comments
- Style demands the linter already enforces
- Praise that is not specific enough to be useful
